Knowing the mechanism of action of a drug may help provide information about the safety of the drug and how it affects the body. It may also help identify the right dose of a drug and which patients are most likely to respond to treatment.

Section.Description: This section summarizes the environmental fate/exposure of this chemical, including the natural and artificial sources of the chemical as a pollutant, its environmental fate, biodegradation, abiotic degradation, bioconcentration, etc.

StringWithMarkup.String: Clonitralide's production and use as a molluscicide and piscicide will result in its release to the environment. If released to soil, clonitralide will have moderate mobility. Volatilization of clonitralide will not be important from moist or dry soil surfaces. Dissociation of the ethanolamine salt of clonitralide should produce ethanolamine and niclosamide. Based on the UV absorption spectra of m-acetoacetanilide, a structurally similar compound, the niclosamide fragment should absorb sunlight and therefore may undergo some direct photolysis on soil and water surfaces. However, clonitralide was found to retain its toxicity for 8 weeks when exposed to full sunlight. The fact that the clonitralide persisted over a year in muds suggests it is not readily biodegraded under water-saturated conditions. If released to water, clonitralide may adsorb to suspended solids and sediment. Clonitralide will be essentially nonvolatile from water surfaces. An estimated BCF value of 46 suggests that bioconcentration of clonitralide will be moderate, not high in aquatic organisms. Hydrolysis of clonitralide should not be important in environmental waters (pHs 5-9). The observed lack of biotransformation of the free amide in soil suggests that biotransformation in water may not be important. However, clonitralide is rapidly degraded in pond sediment with a half-life of 1.1-2.9 days. If released to the atmosphere, clonitralide will exist primarily in the particulate phase. Vapor-phase clonitralide is degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically produced hydroxyl radicals with an estimated half-life of about 4.5 hours. Particulate-phase clonitralide may be physically removed from the air by wet and dry deposition. Because of the presence of a phenolic group, clonitralide may also react quickly in the atmosphere with nitrate radicals. The general population and workers will become exposed to clonitralide through its application and dermal contact to water in which it was applied. (SRC)

Hydrolysis of the free amide in the environment should not be important because the hydrolysis half-life was determined to be 19 days in 0.5N sodium hydroxide solution and it was reported that hydrolysis would be minor in the pH range 5-9(2). Based on the absorption spectrum of structurally similar m-acetoacetanilide which shows weak UV absorption at and above 290 nm(3), photolysis of the amide by sunlight may be important, but rates of photolysis are unknown(SRC). Since clonitralide contains a phenolic group, it may react quickly with nitrate radicals in the atmosphere(4,SRC).

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.
